About this document

This document provides the teaching content for Business Studies Years 12–13 of
the New Zealand Curriculum. Equivalent for Te Marautanga o Aotearoa is being
published separately.

Progress and assessment information for Business Studies Years 12–13 is still in
development. Once that is completed, Business Studies Years 12–13 is proposed to
be made by the Minister of Education as a National Curriculum Statement under
section 90(1)(a) of the Education and Training Act 2020.

It is proposed that, once made and published in the New Zealand Gazette, schools
who offer Business Studies Years 12–13 will be required to start using it in Year 12
from 1 January 2029, and in Year 13 from 1 January 2030.

This document will be replaced with the official version made under the Act and
published in the New Zealand Gazette once that has occurred.

Students are taught core business concepts, frameworks, and practices that explain
how businesses create value, operate, grow, and respond to changing economic,
social, cultural, technological, and environmental conditions. Through the use of
business models, strategic frameworks, financial information, and market evidence,
students examine how businesses manage resources, create competitive advantage,
respond to stakeholder needs, and balance growth, risk, and sustainability.

Business Studies provides students with the knowledge and practices to analyse
business situations, issues, environments, data, and organisational practices using
disciplinary concepts, tools, frameworks, and evidence. This disciplinary knowledge
helps students develop the ability to apply business thinking to interpret information,
examine relationships and impacts, explain outcomes, and support informed decision-
making in local, national, and global contexts.

As students progress through Years 12–13, they develop the ability to evaluate and
synthesise information, perspectives, and evidence, and to communicate reasoned
conclusions using disciplinary language and conventions in written form. This enables
them to justify decisions, develop recommendations and business proposals, and
communicate strategically, ethically, and effectively about complex business issues
and opportunities.

 Disciplinary Writing

 Focus: the use of writing to reflect the ways in which knowledge is organised, analysed, and communicated within the discipline.
 In Business Studies, students use explicitly taught disciplinary writing to analyse, evaluate, justify, and communicate business ideas, decisions, strategies, and outcomes using business concepts,
 frameworks, evidence, data, and terminology.

Context specifications – Years 12 and 13

 Contexts include both:

 •   teacher-provided case studies
 •   student-generated ideas.
 Student-generated ideas may be developed for real-world sale OR explored as innovative concepts that are not taken to market.


 References to businesses include:

 •   agribusinesses – businesses that produce, process, distribute, or support products and services from agriculture, aquaculture, dairy manufacturing, equine, forestry,
     horticulture, seafood, and sports turf industries, and rely directly on biological systems and natural ecosystems
 •   kaupapa Māori businesses – businesses or enterprises that are operated according to traditional or contemporary Māori culture and values. Some kaupapa Māori businesses
     are owner-operated and some employ people of Māori descent. Others may employ people of diverse ethnicities
 •   social enterprises – businesses that generate income while prioritising social, environmental, cultural, or community outcomes, with profits primarily reinvested to support
     their purpose
 •   not-for-profits – organisations that operate for social, cultural, environmental, charitable, sporting, educational, or community purposes and do not distribute profits to private
     owners or shareholders
 •   all New Zealand businesses operating domestically or in a global context.
